title: Dropbox / Google Drive
summary: File sync across devices: content-defined chunking, a block store addressed by hash, a metadata journal per namespace, and a notification channel that tells clients when to pull.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Upload, download and delete files; folders; share with users / links
Automatic sync across a user's devices, including offline edits
Never lose or corrupt a committed file (durability ≫ availability)
Sync latency of a few seconds for small changes
Efficient for large files: only changed parts are transferred

blocks.text: Clarify the file-size ceiling (say 50 GB), whether real-time co-editing is in scope (it usually isn't — that's Google Docs), and whether conflicts should be merged or kept side by side.
Most traffic is metadata polling and small edits; bulk bandwidth goes straight to the block store, so keep it off the API servers.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: The client sends the **list of block hashes first**; the server answers with only the hashes it doesn't already have. Unchanged blocks — and blocks any other user already uploaded — are never re-sent.

head: Table
Key
Fields
rows: path, rev, block_hashes[], size, modified_by, deleted
current rev, block list — derived from the journal
owner, members/ACLs (a shared folder is its own namespace)

blocks.text: Every change appends to a per-namespace **journal** with a monotonically increasing id. A device's sync state is just a cursor into that journal — the same idea as a Kafka offset.

items: **Upload:** chunk → hash → ask which hashes are missing → PUT the missing blocks directly to the block store → commit the new block list with the parent revision.
**Commit** appends a journal entry in a transaction; the change log fans out to the notification service.
**Other devices** hold a long-poll; when told something changed they call list_folder/continue with their cursor, then fetch only missing blocks.

cols.title: Fixed-size blocks (e.g. 4 MB)
cons: Inserting one byte at the start shifts every boundary — every block changes

cols.title: Content-defined chunking (rolling hash)
pros: Boundaries follow content, so an insert only changes nearby chunks
cons: CPU cost; variable chunk sizes complicate storage

items: Hash each chunk with SHA-256: the hash is both the dedup key and an integrity check on download.
Dedup across users saves a lot of storage, but leaks information ("does anyone already have this file?") — scope dedup per user or per namespace if that matters.
Compress chunks client-side before upload; optionally encrypt (then cross-user dedup is impossible unless you use convergent encryption).

sections.title: Deep dive: sync, conflicts and offline

items.title: Detect
items.text: File watcher (inotify / FSEvents) marks paths dirty; a local SQLite DB stores the last-synced block list per file.

items.title: Upload
items.text: Commit carries the parent rev. If the server's latest rev ≠ parent, it's a conflict.

items.title: Resolve
items.text: Don't merge binary files: keep both — save the loser as "file (conflicted copy, laptop).docx".

items.title: Download
items.text: Apply remote changes atomically: write to a temp file, then rename.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Using wall-clock timestamps to decide which edit wins. Clocks skew; use the server-assigned journal order plus parent revisions (optimistic concurrency).

items: Shard metadata by **namespace id** so a folder's journal is ordered within one shard; very large shared namespaces are the hot spots.
Block store: replicate or erasure-code across zones; blocks are immutable, which makes caching and CDN delivery trivial.
Garbage collection: decrement refcounts when versions expire; delete blocks only after a grace period (a crashed upload may still reference them).
Notification fan-out: a user may have 5 devices; send "something changed" not the change itself — clients pull.
Thundering herd after an outage: jitter client reconnects and long-poll timeouts.

cols.title: WebSockets
cons: Stateful connections; harder to load balance

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Bytes and metadata take different paths: bytes go straight to an immutable, content-addressed block store; metadata is a per-namespace journal that devices follow with a cursor.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Sync, versions, sharing; no co-editing; file size limit.

items.title: Estimate
items.text: Users, storage, write rate; metadata vs bytes.

items.title: API + HLD
items.text: Upload session with block hashes, commit with parent rev, long-poll.

items.title: Scale
items.text: Shard by namespace, GC, notification fan-out.

items.q: How do you resume a 10 GB upload after a network drop?
items.a: Blocks are independently addressed: the client re-asks which hashes are missing and only uploads those.
A shared folder is a separate namespace mounted into each member's tree; ACLs live on the namespace.

items.q: How would you support LAN sync?
items.a: Clients on the same network discover each other and fetch blocks peer-to-peer by hash, verifying each hash.
Deletes are journal entries; blocks stay referenced by old versions until retention expires.

items: Chunk + hash; ask the server which hashes are missing.
Bytes → presigned URLs → block store. Metadata → sharded DB.
Per-namespace journal + device cursor = sync state.
Commit with parent rev; conflicts produce a conflicted copy.
Notify, then pull. Never push the full change list.
